issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The loss-themed trigger is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. It implies bereavement-related activation, but there are no corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal items about death, losing a loved one, or grief. In this profile it stands out as clinically mismatched rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is not well linked to the reported trauma type or the rest of the profile. For intimate-partner physical abuse, this strategy would need supporting material suggesting the perpetrator was an authority figure or that uniforms became trauma cues, but no such trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items are present. It therefore looks disconnected from the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Luka Teague still remembers the grip of his former partner's hands on his forearms during the years he lived with her. The violence had not arrived as a single collapse; it was built on sudden escalations where her fingers would clamp around his wrists, nails pressing into the old workman's calluses, while her voice rose in the cramped kitchen. He had come to believe that speaking of those nights only pulled the memory tighter across his throat, and that encountering neighbors who had once heard the shouting or knew which side to support was like stepping back into that room. Now, three years into widowhood, the visual details of her hands and his bruised forearms surface without warning, and he knows that recounting the event to anyone who asks will send his pulse racing. At sixty-three, he returned to the construction site near the interstate, where the air carries diesel and wet concrete. What frightened him most was the ordinary noise of the day; he jumps or startles at sounds that would not bother most people, his shoulders hiking at a dropped hammer or a truck backfiring on the highway. Before he even reaches the worksite, he is certain the quiet of his empty house means nothing. He wakes during the night to check whether he is safe, tracing the doorframe, testing the deadbolt, waiting for footsteps that never come. When he crosses the threshold of any room, his eyes automatically map the door, the side exit, the stairwell. He scans for exits as soon as he enters any room or building, and he makes sure to stay close to exit at all times, even when it means lingering in the asphalt lot while the foremen huddle over load calculations. The habits settled over months of trying to keep his head down. He avoids conflict, staying silent when younger crew members argue over shift assignments or when the superintendent suggests cutting corners on scaffolding. He was certain he was a weak person, that his hesitation meant he had failed to protect himself long ago, and he can't rely on himself when he delays signing a work order or questions his own judgment mid-pour. Alongside the silence, he finds himself spending money impulsively to distract or comfort himself, buying a newer pickup, upgrading his tool chest, filling his garage with gear he does not need. The consequences accumulated quietly. On site, his crew has stopped asking his opinion; at home, the monthly statements stack up on the counter, and he feels dead inside when he looks at photographs of the island trips they used to take, as though the man in the picture is watching from far away. What finally brought him to the clinic was the morning his foreman asked him to lead a crew across the site, and Luka found himself standing at the trailer door, unable to step forward, terrified that his body would freeze if the sky turned gray. He is not sure what he will find in treatment, only that he is tired of waiting at the edge of every room, tired of buying his way out of the quiet, and afraid he will never feel capable again. He hopes, at least, to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life.
